ask: Which of the following describes a corrective control?
options: It restores operations after an event
It substitutes for a safeguard that cannot be used
It blocks an event before it happens
It tells people what they must do
why: Corrective controls act after an event to limit damage and return to normal.
That describes a compensating control.
That describes a preventive control.
That describes a directive control.

ask: Which of the following controls is corrective?
options: An isolated network for an old system
why: Isolating a system that cannot take the ideal control is compensating.
A sign that instructs is directive.
Restoring data after an event returns operations to normal.
Reviewing logs identifies events, which is detective.

stem: Malware wiped the order database at a bicycle wholesaler on Tuesday. On Wednesday the database administrator loaded Monday's copy, and the company resumed taking orders.
ask: Which of the following control types does loading Monday's copy provide?
why: Nothing stands in for a missing control; the damage is being repaired.
Loading the saved copy repairs the damage after the event and restores operations.
Finding the damage would be detective; loading the copy repairs it.
The attack already happened, so nothing is being blocked.

stem: After an attacker used a flaw in a hotel's booking site, the incident response lead removed the attacker's files and installed the vendor's fix for the flaw.
ask: Which of the following control types do the lead's actions provide?
why: The flaw was already exploited, so the fix repairs rather than blocks an attack that already happened.
The lead applied the real fix, not a substitute for a control that cannot be used.
The actions remove and fix; they do not identify the event.
Removing the attacker's files and patching the hole after the attack is corrective.

stem: A help desk technician at a university learns that an intruder has already signed in to a professor's account with a password that was posted on a public forum, and resets that password at once.
ask: Which of the following control types does the reset provide?
why: The intruder has already used the account; the reset repairs that compromise after the event instead of blocking it before it happens.
Learning about the intruder's sign-in is detective; the reset is the repair.
The reset does not tell anyone what to do.
The intruder has already signed in with the password; resetting it removes that access after the event.

stem: Malware spread from an old controller at a packaging factory. The plant's control engineer cleaned the controller and, because it cannot run security software, moved it to an isolated network segment.
ask: Which of the following control types describes cleaning the controller?
why: The move to an isolated segment is compensating, but the stem asks about cleaning the controller.
Cleaning the controller repairs damage after the event.
Cleaning does not identify the event; it repairs it.
Cleaning does not instruct anyone.

stem: A scan at a school finds a remote access trojan on a teacher's laptop. The IT staff then wipe the laptop and reinstall it from a clean image.
ask: Which of the following control types does the reinstall provide?
why: Wiping and reinstalling removes the infection and returns the laptop to a clean state.
The scan that found the trojan is detective; the reinstall repairs.
The laptop was already infected, so nothing is being blocked.
Nothing stands in for a missing control.

stem: The security engineer at a web host finds that a customer site's private key was copied last week and has since been used to impersonate the customer's site and collect visitors' passwords. The engineer revokes the site's certificate that afternoon.
ask: Which of the following control types does revoking the certificate provide?
why: The copied key has already been misused; revoking repairs that compromise rather than blocking an attack before it starts.
Finding the copied key is detective; revoking the certificate is the repair.
The key was already misused, so revoking the certificate limits the damage after the event.
Revoking discourages no one; it cancels the compromised certificate.

stem: An incident handler at a car rental company writes the record below.
ask: Which of the following control types does the 11:45 entry record?

lines: 09:12  INC-3307 opened: ransom note found on shared drive S
09:30  Shared drive S taken offline
11:45  Shared drive S restored from the 02:00 snapshot, users reconnected

why: The ransom note being found at 09:12 is detection; 11:45 restores service.
Restoring the drive from a snapshot returns operations to normal after the event.
The attack already happened; nothing is being blocked.
Nothing stands in for a missing control.

stem: A clothing store's checkout server was infected with malware last night. The manager asks for the controls that limit the damage now and bring the server back.
ask: Which of the following meet the request? (Select TWO)
options: Removing the malware from the server
Showing a login banner on the server
Restoring the server from a clean backup
Banning personal USB drives by policy
Adding a malware alert rule to the server
why: Removing the infection after the event limits the damage.
A warning banner discourages future misuse; it repairs nothing.
Restoring returns the server to normal operation after the event.
A policy tells people what to do in the future; it repairs nothing now.
An alert identifies a future event; it does not bring the server back.

ask: Which of the following describes a technical control?
options: Staff carry it out as daily work
Leadership sets it in a written policy
A barrier guards a room or building
why: Technical controls run in hardware, software or firmware, so the system applies them rather than a person.
That describes an operational control, which people perform.
That describes a managerial control, made of policies and risk decisions.
That describes a physical control, which protects tangible spaces.

ask: Which of the following is another name for the technical control category?
why: Administrative is the other name for managerial, not technical.
Operational is its own category, for controls people carry out.
Physical is its own category, for controls that protect spaces and assets.
Logical is another name for the technical category.

stem: The systems administrator at a law firm sets the file server so that only members of the litigation group can open the case folders. Requests from anyone else are refused by the operating system.
ask: Which of the following control categories does this describe?
why: No document or risk decision does the work; the server refuses the requests itself.
No person checks each request.
Operating system permissions are enforced by the system on every request.
Nothing guards a room or device; the protection is on the folders.

stem: Two controls protect the payroll database at a freight company. An analyst reads the database's access report every Friday, and the database encrypts every record it stores.
ask: Which of the following control categories fits the record encryption?
why: That fits the Friday report reading, which a person performs; the encryption needs no person.
No policy or risk decision is described for the encryption.
The database applies the encryption itself, so a system enforces it.
Encryption protects data, not a room or piece of equipment.

stem: The IT coordinator at a school district has the district's laptops run antivirus software that quarantines a harmful download the moment it arrives, before any staff member looks at it.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the antivirus software belong to?
why: No staff member is involved; the software acts on its own.
The software is not a policy or a risk decision.
It protects files on the laptop, not a space or the laptop as an object.
The software acts by itself the moment the file arrives, which is a system enforcing a rule.

stem: A network engineer at a hotel group writes a rule that blocks remote desktop connections from outside. The edge firewall now applies it to every incoming connection.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the firewall applying the rule?
why: Deciding what the rule should be can be managerial, but the stem asks about the firewall applying it.
Once written, the rule is applied by the firewall to every connection with no person deciding.
Writing the rule is a one-time act by a person; applying it is done by the firewall.
The rule filters network traffic; nothing guards a room or device.

stem: The compliance officer at a health insurer sends a supplier a questionnaire asking it to list its logical controls that protect member data.
ask: Which of the following controls belongs under that heading?
why: Logical is another name for technical, and permissions are enforced by the system.
A policy is managerial, also called administrative, not logical.
Locked cabinets protect tangible items, which is physical.
Training is carried out by people, which is operational, not logical.

stem: The network administrator at a travel agency sets the VPN gateway to refuse any laptop whose device certificate is on the revocation list, even when the user types the right password.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the gateway's refusal?
why: The gateway checks every connection against the revocation list by itself, so a system enforces the rule.
Nothing guards a room, a site or a piece of equipment; the check happens over the network.
No person looks at each connection; the gateway decides on its own.
Putting a certificate on the list may follow a policy, but the refusal itself is carried out by the gateway.

stem: A network administrator at a county library reviews two lines that the edge firewall applies to all traffic.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes these lines?

lines: rule 10  permit tcp any host 198.51.100.20 eq 443
rule 20  deny   ip  any host 198.51.100.20

why: The lines are enforced by a device; they are not a policy document or a risk decision.
No person checks each connection.
The firewall enforces the lines on every packet with no person deciding.
The lines filter network traffic; nothing guards a room or device.

stem: The security lead at a physiotherapy practice must list two technical controls for an upcoming audit.
ask: Which of the following belong on the list? (Select TWO)
options: A visitor sign-in sheet at reception
why: People fill in and check a sign-in sheet; no system enforces it.
Encryption is applied by the laptop itself, so a system enforces it.
A risk assessment is a managerial control.
The system locks the account by itself after the failed attempts.
Locks protect a space, which is a physical control.

ask: Which of the following describes a physical control?
options: Software enforces a rule on a system
Staff carry out a routine task
A barrier guards rooms or equipment
why: That describes a technical control.
That describes an operational control.
That describes a managerial control.
Physical controls limit access to tangible spaces and assets.

ask: Which of the following controls belongs to the physical category?
why: Firewall rules are enforced by a system, which is technical.
Bollards are posts that protect a building or space, a physical control.
Staff reviewing logs is operational work.
A risk assessment is a managerial control.

stem: The operations manager of a stadium installs a row of steel posts in front of its ticket office so that no vehicle can reach the windows.
ask: Which of the following control categories do the steel posts belong to?
why: The posts are a tangible barrier protecting a building.
The posts enforce nothing through software or firmware; they are a barrier.
No person performs a task; the posts work by being there.
The posts are not a policy or a risk decision.

stem: The facilities manager at a data center fits a lock to every server rack and gives the keys to only two engineers.
ask: Which of the following control categories do the rack locks belong to?
why: Deciding who holds keys is a managerial choice, but the locks themselves protect the equipment.
No routine task is described; the locks work by being there.
Rack locks limit physical access to equipment.
A key lock involves no software or firmware enforcing a rule.

stem: The owner of a pawn shop fits fixed steel bars over the shop's ground-floor windows so that no one can get in through the glass from the street.
ask: Which of the following control categories do the window bars belong to?
why: No system or software enforces anything; plain steel bars stand in the way.
The bars put something tangible in the way to protect the building.
No one performs a routine task; the bars work on their own.
The bars are not a policy or risk decision.

stem: The security manager at a car plant has a booth built at its only vehicle gate, with a barrier arm that stays down until a guard clears each vehicle.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the booth and barrier arm?
why: A booth and a barrier arm are tangible structures controlling entry to the site.
The guard who clears each vehicle does operational work, but the ask is about the booth and the arm.
No software rule is described; the arm is a barrier.
Neither is a policy or a risk decision.

stem: The facilities manager at a broadcaster installs a gas fire suppression system and a backup generator in the room that holds its transmission servers.
ask: Which of the following control categories do these protections belong to?
why: They do not enforce access or data rules through software; they protect the room and its power.
No routine task performed by people is described.
Neither is a policy or a risk decision.
Fire suppression and backup power protect the physical environment of the servers.

stem: The site manager at a cattle feed company puts a three-meter fence topped with wire around its yard so that intruders cannot climb in.
ask: Which of the following classifies the fence correctly?
why: The labels are swapped: physical is a category and preventive is a type.
No person performs a task; the fence is a tangible barrier, so the category is physical.
A fence is physical by category, and stopping intruders climbing in is preventive.
Corrective acts after an event to repair damage; the fence stops intruders beforehand.

stem: The owner of a parking garage fits bright lights on every level and in every stairwell so that the whole building stays well lit at night.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the lighting belong to?
why: No software or firmware enforces a rule here.
No person performs a routine task; the lights work by being on.
Lighting protects a tangible space, which is a physical control.
Lighting is not a policy or risk decision.

stem: The practice manager at a clinic must add two physical controls to protect the room where it keeps medicines.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: A policy limiting who may enter
A locked door with a badge reader
Weekly stock counts by a pharmacist
Alerts when the stock database changes
A steel grille over the room window
why: A policy is a managerial control.
A lock and badge reader control entry to the room, which is physical.
A person counting stock is operational work.
Alerts generated by a system are technical.
A grille physically blocks entry through the window, which is physical.

ask: What makes a control managerial?
options: A system enforcing a rule by itself
A policy or risk decision guiding security
A lock or fence guarding a space
why: That describes a technical control.
Managerial controls design and oversee security through policies, standards and risk assessments.
That describes an operational control.
That describes a physical control.

ask: Which of the following control categories is also called administrative?
why: The other name for technical is logical.
Operational controls are carried out by people; they have no administrative alias.
Physical controls protect spaces and assets; they are not called administrative.
Administrative is the other name for managerial controls.

stem: The chief executive of a seed company approves an offboarding policy. It says every departing employee's accounts must be closed on their last day.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the approved policy belong to?
why: The accounts may be closed in a system later, but the policy itself is a document, not technology.
Staff closing the accounts would be operational; the policy sets the rule they follow.
A policy protects no room or piece of equipment.
An offboarding policy approved by leadership is a managerial control.

stem: The chief risk officer at a card payment processor hires an outside firm to rate the likelihood and impact of each threat to its payment systems. The results go to the board.
ask: Which of the following control categories fits this exercise?
why: The firm rates risks for leadership; this is oversight, not routine security work done by staff.
A risk assessment that informs leadership is a managerial control.
No system enforces anything; the output is a set of ratings.
Nothing protects a space or a piece of equipment.

stem: The chief risk officer at a museum keeps a risk register that lists each risk, its owner and the decision the board took about it.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the risk register fall under?
why: The register records who owns each risk and what was decided, which is managerial oversight.
The register is not hands-on daily work; it records how risks are owned and decided.
The register enforces nothing; it is a record of decisions.
It protects no space or equipment.

stem: The chief executive of a regional bank decides that every employee must complete security awareness training each year and approves funding for the program.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the chief executive's decision?
why: Delivering the training to staff is operational, but the stem asks about the decision to require it.
No system enforces anything here.
Requiring training and funding a program is a governance decision, which is managerial.
Nothing protects a space or equipment.

stem: The procurement director at a logistics firm issues a standard that no new supplier may be signed until it has met a list of security requirements.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the director's standard belong to?
why: No one performs a routine task here; the standard sets requirements for suppliers.
Setting security requirements that suppliers must meet is a governance decision, which is managerial.
No system enforces the standard.
A standard protects no space or equipment.

stem: A security analyst at a cosmetics maker receives the message below from the security office.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the message announce?

lines: From: security-office@cosmetics.example
Subject: New standard for customer data
From 1 March, customer files may be stored only in the approved document vault.

why: The message sets a new standard for how data is stored, which is managerial.
The vault may enforce access later, but the message sets a standard; it enforces nothing itself.
No routine task performed by people is described; a standard is set.
The standard protects files, not a room or piece of equipment.

stem: Each year, the chief information security officer at a shipping firm compares the results of the firm's security program with the goals set for it and decides what to fund next.
ask: Which of the following control categories does this yearly review fall under?
why: This is not routine security work on systems; it is leadership overseeing the program.
No system enforces anything; leadership is making decisions.
Nothing protects a space or equipment.
Reviewing results against goals and deciding what to fund is oversight of security, which is managerial.

stem: The chair of a hospital's governance committee asks the security team for a list of its managerial controls.
ask: Which of the following belong on the list? (Select TWO)
options: Weekly log review by an analyst
why: Guards are people doing security work on site, not a policy or risk decision.
Antivirus is enforced by software, which is technical.
A standard that guides how data is handled is managerial.
A person reviewing logs is operational work.
A risk assessment is a typical managerial control.

ask: What is the purpose of a detective control?
options: It blocks an event before it starts
It identifies and records an event
It repairs damage after an event
why: That describes a preventive control.
That describes a deterrent control.
Detective controls identify and record events so they can be investigated, without stopping them.
That describes a corrective control.

ask: Which of the following controls is detective?
options: A firewall rule that drops inbound traffic
A motion sensor that trips an alarm
A banner warning that misuse is prosecuted
why: Dropping traffic blocks it, which is preventive.
The sensor identifies movement and raises an alarm.
A warning banner discourages, which is deterrent.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

stem: A database administrator at a mail-order nursery adds a fake customer record that no genuine process ever opens, and tells no one outside the security team that it exists. If anyone reads the record, a message goes to the security inbox, but the read still completes.
ask: Which of the following control types does the fake record provide?
why: The record identifies and records the access and raises an alert without stopping it.
The read still completes, so nothing was blocked.
The record is kept secret, so it cannot discourage anyone.
Nothing is repaired; an alert is raised.

stem: A museum's motion sensors sound an alarm at the night guard's desk when someone moves through a closed gallery after hours.
ask: Which of the following control types do the motion sensors provide?
why: The sensors lock nothing; the person can still move through the gallery.
The sensors work whether or not anyone knows of them; their job is to report movement.
Nothing is repaired; an alarm is raised.
The sensors identify movement and raise an alarm.

stem: A clinic's camera is hidden above a ceiling tile in the drug store room. Each morning a manager reviews its footage to see who entered overnight.
ask: Which of the following control types does the hidden camera serve?
why: A hidden camera cannot discourage anyone who does not know it is there.
The camera does not stop anyone entering.
The footage is reviewed to identify who entered, which is detective.
Reviewing footage repairs nothing.

stem: The network engineer at a hospital connects a sensor to a copy of its network traffic. The sensor alerts the security team when it sees an attack pattern, but it has no way to drop traffic.
ask: Which of the following control types does the sensor provide?
why: It cannot drop traffic, so it blocks nothing.
An alert repairs nothing.
The sensor identifies attacks and alerts, which is detective.
The sensor is not described as a substitute for a missing control.

stem: A help desk technician at a shipping firm gets a report from the endpoint tool that a laptop is infected with malware. The removal is scheduled for the next morning.
ask: Which of the following control types did the endpoint tool's report provide?
why: Removing the malware tomorrow is corrective; the report only identified it.
The malware is already on the laptop, so nothing was blocked.
The report does not stand in for a missing control.
The report identified the infection, which is detective.

stem: The systems engineer at an energy company runs a monitoring tool that keeps a fingerprint of each configuration file on its control servers and sends an alert when a fingerprint changes.
ask: Which of the following control types does the monitoring tool provide?
why: The tool does not stop the file being changed.
The tool identifies a changed file and alerts after the change.
The tool does not tell anyone what to do; it reports a change.
The tool restores nothing; it alerts.

stem: An analyst at a property management company reads the entries below.
ask: Which of the following control types does the last entry show at work?

lines: 08:41:02 sshd: Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.77
08:41:09 sshd: Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.77
08:41:19 sshd: Accepted password for admin from 203.0.113.77
08:41:20 monitor: rule 'failures then success' fired, ticket 5521 opened

why: The rule identified the pattern and opened a ticket after it happened.
The login was accepted, so nothing was blocked.
Opening a ticket repairs nothing; locking the account afterward would be corrective.
No warning was shown to the attacker; the rule fired after the fact.

stem: An internal auditor at an insurer finds no way to learn that a break-in at the records room has happened. The auditor asks for controls that identify and record such events.
ask: Which of the following meet the auditor's request? (Select TWO)
options: A stronger lock on the door
A sign warning that intruders are prosecuted
A motion sensor wired to the alarm panel
A door access log reviewed every morning
A procedure for replacing stolen files
why: A lock blocks entry, which is preventive, and records nothing.
A warning sign discourages, which is deterrent.
The sensor identifies movement in the room and raises an alarm.
A reviewed access log records entries and lets people spot a break-in.
Replacing what was taken is corrective, after the event.

ask: Which of the following explains how a directive control works?
options: It enforces a rule so no one can break it
It instructs people and relies on compliance
It warns of consequences to discourage misuse
It restores systems after an incident has happened
why: Enforcing so the act cannot happen is preventive.
Directive controls tell people what to do and rely on them to comply.
Warning of consequences to discourage misuse describes a deterrent control.
Restoring after an incident is corrective.

ask: Which of the following controls is directive?
options: A door that locks itself whenever it closes
A sign warning that trespassers will be prosecuted
An alarm that sounds when a door opens
A policy telling staff where to store files
why: A self-locking door blocks entry, which is preventive.
Warning of consequences is deterrent.
An alarm identifies an event, which is detective.
A policy that states required behavior is directive.

stem: A contractor visiting a pharmaceutical plant sees a sign at a lab door reading 'Lab staff only beyond this point.' The door itself is not locked.
ask: Which of the following control types does the sign provide?
why: The door is not locked, so nothing stops anyone entering.
The sign names no consequence; it only says who may enter.
The sign records nothing and raises no alert.
The sign tells people who may enter and relies on them to comply.

stem: A newspaper's handbook says reporters must lock their screens whenever they step away from their desks. The computers do not lock by themselves.
ask: Which of the following control types does the handbook rule provide?
why: Nothing locks the screens automatically, so nothing is blocked.
The rule tells reporters what to do and relies on them to do it.
No consequence is stated; the handbook only says what to do.
Nothing has happened that needs repair.

stem: A forklift trainer at a warehouse points out two signs near the racking. One reads 'Forklift drivers only beyond the yellow line.' The other reads 'Violators will be fined.'
ask: Which of the following control types does the first sign provide?
why: The first sign says who may go where and relies on compliance.
That fits the second sign, which warns of a fine.
A sign stops no one crossing the line.
Neither sign records anything.

stem: The office manager at a design studio notes that the studio's acceptable use policy forbids installing unapproved apps. Later, the studio adds a tool that refuses to run any app not on an approved list.
ask: Which of the following control types does the acceptable use policy provide?
why: That fits the tool that refuses unapproved apps, not the policy.
The policy records nothing and raises no alert.
The policy states required behavior and relies on staff to comply.
The policy repairs nothing after an event.

stem: The vendor manager at a bank adds a clause to the contract with its cloud provider requiring the provider to keep the bank's data only in data centers inside the country.
ask: Which of the following control types does the contract clause provide?
why: The clause discovers nothing; it states a duty.
The clause states what the provider must do and relies on it to comply.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.
Nothing in the clause technically stops the data from being moved; it relies on the provider to comply.

stem: An airline's policy says staff must not share their accounts. Nothing in its systems blocks sharing, and auditors later find shared accounts in several teams.
ask: Which of the following explains why the policy did not stop the sharing?
options: It relies on people choosing to comply
It acts only after the sharing happens
It records sharing but raises no alert
It stands in for a missing control
why: A directive control instructs but does not enforce, so people can ignore it.
Acting after an event describes a corrective control, not a policy.
A policy records nothing; recording an event would be detective.
Standing in for a missing control describes compensating, not this policy.

stem: The receptionist at a marine supply company receives the notice below.
ask: Which of the following control types does the notice provide?

lines: From: security@harbor.example
To: all staff
From Monday, every visitor must be signed in at the front desk and escorted at all times.

why: The notice states no consequence for ignoring it.
Nothing in the notice physically stops an unescorted visitor.
The notice records nothing.
The notice tells staff what must happen and relies on them to comply.

stem: The compliance lead at a tax advisory firm wants to add two directive controls for how staff handle client tax returns.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: A lock on the cabinet holding paper returns
A log that records each return a user opens
A policy to save returns only in the protected folder
A notice warning that leaks will be prosecuted
A guide listing the steps for emailing returns securely
why: A lock stops anyone without a key from opening the cabinet, which is preventive.
A log records what happened, which is detective.
A policy tells staff where to save returns and relies on them to comply, which is directive.
A warning of consequences is deterrent.
A guide tells staff what to do and relies on them to follow it, which is directive.

ask: Which of the following does a security control type describe?
options: How severe the threat it faces is
why: How a control is implemented is its category, a separate label.
Threat severity belongs to risk analysis; a type names the goal the control serves.
The protected asset does not decide the type; the goal does.
A type names the job a control does: prevent, deter, detect, correct, compensate or direct.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

ask: Which of the following lists only control types?
why: Technical and physical are categories, not types.
All three are control types: stop it, identify it, fix it after.
These are all categories, which describe how a control is implemented.
Physical is a category, not a type.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A hotel posts a guard at its service entrance. The guard turns away anyone without a staff badge and writes down the name of every person who passes.
ask: Which of the following control types does the guard serve? (Select TWO)
why: Turning away people without a badge stops them entering.
Nothing has gone wrong that needs repair.
The guard is not standing in for a control that cannot be used.
The guard enforces entry rather than only telling people what to do.
Writing down every person who passes records events for later investigation.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: An auditor at a shipping line asks what goal the new alarm on the loading dock door serves. The alarm sounds and logs an entry when the door opens after hours, but it does not lock anything.
ask: Which of the following answers the auditor's question?
why: The alarm identifies and records the door opening, which is the detective goal.
Physical is a category, how the control is implemented; the auditor asked what goal it serves.
The alarm does not lock anything, so it blocks nothing.
Technical is a category, not a goal; the auditor asked for the type.

source.chapter: Classifying one control by category and type (worked method)

stem: The fleet manager at a courier company puts stickers on every van stating that no cash is kept inside, so that thieves will not bother trying. The stickers do not lock the vans or record anything.
ask: Which of the following control types do the stickers serve?
why: The stickers try to discourage thieves without stopping them.
The stickers lock nothing, and preventive controls actually block.
The stickers record nothing and raise no alert.
No break-in has happened that needs repair.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A security architect's design review of a bank's mobile app finds strong controls that block attacks, but nothing that would reveal when an attack gets through.
ask: Which of the following control types is missing?
why: The review says the blocking controls are already strong.
Discouraging attackers would not reveal an attack that got through.
Detective controls identify and record events, which is what the review found missing.
Telling people what to do would not reveal an attack that got through.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: The manager of a city parking lot mounts large, obvious cameras at each entrance with a sign naming them. The stated reason is to make car thieves choose another lot.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the stated reason for the cameras?
why: The cameras also record, which is detective, but the stated reason is to make thieves go elsewhere.
Making thieves choose another lot is discouraging the attempt, which is deterrence.
Cameras do not physically stop anyone entering.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: The engineering manager at a software firm writes in the handbook that developers must not paste customer data into chat tools. Nothing in the chat tools blocks it.
ask: Which of the following control types does the handbook rule provide?
why: Nothing in the tools blocks the pasting, so nothing is prevented.
The rule records nothing and raises no alert.
The rule is not standing in for a control that cannot be used.
The rule tells people what not to do and relies on them to comply.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: The chief engineer at a ferry operator plans three controls for the engine room: a warning sign on the door, a lock on the door, and a sensor that alerts the bridge when the door opens.
ask: Which of the following control types does the sensor provide?
why: That is the warning sign's job; the sensor reports what happens.
That is the lock's job; the sensor blocks nothing.
The sensor repairs nothing after an event.
The sensor identifies the door opening and alerts, which is detective.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

stem: A security trainer at a regional airport checks a slide about control types before a staff session.
ask: Which of the following statements on the slide are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: Preventive acts only after an incident
One control can serve several types
Deterrent discourages but does not stop
Compensating repairs damage after an attack
why: Preventive acts before an incident; corrective acts after.
A guard, for example, can prevent, deter and detect at once.
Deterrent works on the attacker's choice; preventive actually blocks.
Directive only instructs people and relies on them to comply.
Repairing after an attack is corrective; compensating substitutes for a missing control.

source.chapter: Preventive vs deterrent vs detective vs corrective vs compensating vs directive (control types compared)

ask: Which of the following does a control's category (technical, managerial, operational or physical) describe?
options: How much risk the control leaves
How likely the threat is to occur
why: A category sorts a control by how it is carried out: by a system, by policy, by people or by a physical barrier.
The goal (stop, discourage, detect and so on) is the control type, a separate label from the category.
The risk left after a control is a risk measure, not a category; categories sort controls by how they are implemented.
Likelihood belongs to risk analysis; categories sort controls by how they are implemented.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

ask: Which of the following lists the four security control categories?
why: Financial is not a control category, and physical, for controls that protect spaces and equipment, is missing.
Logical is another name for technical, so this list repeats one category and leaves out managerial.
These four cover controls enforced by systems, set by policy, done by people and built into the physical space.
Hardware, software and firmware are what a technical control is built from, not separate categories.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: The chief operating officer of a hospital approves a written rule that every visitor must wear a visitor badge at all times while inside the building.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the approved rule belong to?
why: No system enforces anything here; the control is a decision written down.
An approved rule is a policy decision, which is the managerial category.
The badge is a tangible item, but the control asked about is the approved rule, which is a document.
Staff checking badges would be operational, but the rule itself is a governing document.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: The operations manager at a city water utility assigns two staff members to watch the plant's network alerts around the clock and phone the engineer on duty when one looks real.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes this arrangement?
why: The alerts come from systems, but the arrangement is people judging them, not a system enforcing a rule.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is routine work done by staff.
Nothing here protects a building, room or piece of equipment.
People watching alerts and deciding when to call is security work carried out by people day to day.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: The manager of a bus depot surrounds its overnight parking yard with a tall fence that has a single gate.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the fence belong to?
why: No hardware, software or firmware enforces a rule here; the fence is a barrier.
No person performs a task; the fence works simply by being there.
A fence is not a policy or a risk decision.
A fence protects a tangible space, which is the physical category.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: A security standard written by a retailer's security manager states that every laptop must use disk encryption. The IT team then turns on the built-in encryption feature on each laptop.
ask: Which of the following gives the categories of the standard and of the encryption feature, in that order?
why: This reverses them: the standard is the managerial control and the feature is the technical one.
The standard is a governing document (managerial); the encryption is enforced by the laptop itself (technical).
The standard is a governing document, not a routine task people perform.
Disk encryption is enforced by software on the laptop, not by a barrier around a space.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: Password resets at a telecom provider used to need a help desk agent to confirm each caller. Now a self-service portal checks a one-time code and resets the password with no agent involved.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the identity check now?
why: The portal checks the code by itself with no person deciding, so a system enforces it.
It was operational while an agent confirmed callers, but no person performs the check any more.
No policy or risk decision is described; the change is in who performs the check.
Nothing here protects a space or a piece of equipment.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: An auditor sorting a bakery chain's controls places 'antivirus on every till' under the people category because cashiers use the tills all day.
ask: Which of the following control categories should the auditor have used?
why: Cashiers use the tills, but they do not carry out the antivirus control; the software does.
The tills are equipment, but antivirus protects them through software, not a barrier.
Antivirus software works by itself on each till, with no person deciding each case.
Antivirus is not a policy or a risk decision.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

stem: A security administrator at an electric cooperative exports the control register below.
ask: Which of the following control categories applies to CTRL-07?

lines: CTRL-07  Acceptable use document signed by each new hire
CTRL-12  Badge reader on the data hall door
CTRL-19  Endpoint agent blocks unsigned programs
CTRL-23  Help desk calls the user back before a reset

why: That fits CTRL-19, where the endpoint agent enforces the rule; CTRL-07 is a document.
An acceptable use document is a policy that guides behavior, which is managerial.
That fits CTRL-12, the badge reader on a door; CTRL-07 protects no space.
That fits CTRL-23, a task the help desk performs; CTRL-07 is a policy.

stem: A new security analyst at a ferry company drafts notes on the control categories for a team briefing.
ask: Which of the following notes are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: Operational means people carry the control out
Physical means a system enforces the rule
A category names the goal a control serves
why: Operational controls are performed by people in daily work.
A system enforcing a rule is technical; physical controls protect spaces and assets.
Administrative is the other name for the managerial category.
Written policies are managerial; technical controls are enforced by hardware, software or firmware.
The goal is the control type; the category is how the control is implemented.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

ask: Which of the following describes an operational control?
options: A system enforces it with no person
Leadership decides it in a policy
People perform it in daily work
A barrier protects a room or site
why: That describes a technical control.
That describes a managerial control.
Operational controls are carried out by people as part of daily operations.
That describes a physical control.

ask: Which of the following controls is operational?
options: Locks on the server room doors
why: Antivirus is software enforcing rules by itself, which is technical.
A written policy is managerial.
Training is delivered and followed by people, which makes it operational.
Locks protect a space, which is physical.

stem: At a call center, a supervisor walks the floor at the end of each shift and checks that no customer printouts are left on desks.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the supervisor's check?
why: Nothing tangible blocks access here; a person performs the check.
A rule about printouts would be managerial, but the walk is the work itself.
No system enforces the check.
A person performing a routine check during daily operations is operational.

stem: At a pharmaceutical warehouse, the receptionists compare each visitor's photo ID with the expected visitor list by hand and phone the visitor's host before signing the visitor in.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the receptionists' checks?
why: Nothing tangible blocks entry or watches an area; the control is the checking work the receptionists do.
The receptionists perform the ID check and the call by hand as part of their daily work.
No system makes the decision; the receptionists compare IDs and phone hosts themselves.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is a task performed at the desk.

stem: Each morning, an analyst at an online retailer reads the previous night's login records and flags anything unusual to her manager.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the morning review belong to?
why: A person reviewing records as part of daily work is operational.
The records come from systems, but a person reads and judges them.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is routine work.
Nothing protects a space or a device.

stem: When an employee at a staffing agency asks for access to the finance share, an administrator phones the employee's manager to confirm the request before granting it.
ask: Which of the following explains why the phone confirmation is an operational control?
options: A person performs the check by hand
A written rule makes the check happen
why: The administrator makes the call as part of daily work, which is what makes it operational.
No system decides anything; the administrator chooses to call and judges the answer.
A rule requiring confirmation would be managerial, but the stem describes the call itself.
The call protects access to a file share, not a room or building.

stem: A trainer at a city council runs hands-on sessions in which staff practice spotting and reporting suspicious emails.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the sessions?
why: Deciding to require training is managerial, but the stem describes sessions being delivered.
No system enforces anything; a trainer and staff do the work.
Delivering training to staff is security work people carry out, which is operational.
Nothing protects a space or equipment.

stem: Each morning, the night operator at an insurance broker reads the backup report and reruns by hand any backup job that failed overnight.
ask: Which of the following explains why this task is an operational control?
options: A system carries it out with no person
A person does it as routine work
A written policy makes it happen
A barrier guards a room or building
why: The backup software runs the jobs, but the control asked about is the operator reading the report and rerunning failures.
The operator does the check and the rerun by hand every morning, which is operational.
No policy or risk decision is described; the stem describes daily work.
The task protects no space or equipment from physical access.

stem: A system administrator at a seaport keeps the shift checklist below.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the 07:00 entry?

lines: 06:00  Night shift handover signed
06:15  Server room door checked and found locked
07:00  Yesterday's firewall rule changes compared by hand with approved tickets, 1 change queried

why: The firewall itself is technical, but the 07:00 entry is a comparison the administrator makes by hand.
The 06:15 entry concerns a door; the 07:00 entry concerns firewall changes and tickets.
Approving changes is not what the entry records; it records a routine comparison on the shift.
A person checks each change against its ticket as part of the shift's routine, which is operational.

stem: The manager of a distribution center must add two controls in the operational category before the next audit.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: Shift leads counting scanners back in nightly
A badge reader on the warehouse door
An acceptable use policy for handheld scanners
Supervisors reviewing camera footage each shift
why: Shift leads counting the scanners back in is a routine task people do, which is operational.
A badge reader on a door is a physical control.
A policy is a managerial control.
People reviewing footage on a schedule is operational work.
The system locks the account by itself, which is technical.

ask: Which of the following describes a deterrent control?
options: It blocks an attempt before it starts
It discourages but does not stop
It identifies an event and raises an alert
It repairs systems after an incident
why: That describes a preventive control.
A deterrent works on the attacker's choice and does not block the attempt.
That describes a detective control.
That describes a corrective control.

ask: Which of the following controls is a deterrent?
options: A login banner warning of prosecution
A firewall rule blocking inbound traffic
why: A warning of prosecution discourages misuse but does not block a login.
Blocking traffic is preventive.
An alert identifies an event, which is detective.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

stem: The IT director at a software company adds a notice to every staff login screen saying that misuse can lead to dismissal. Staff can still sign in and use the system as normal.
ask: Which of the following control types does the notice serve?
why: The notice warns of a consequence to discourage misuse without blocking anyone.
The notice blocks nothing; staff still sign in as normal.
The notice itself records nothing and raises no alert.
Nothing has happened that needs repair.

stem: The office manager at an architecture firm places a uniformed guard at the reception desk. The manager says the main reason is so that people with bad intentions decide not to try entering.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the stated reason for the guard?
why: A guard can also block entry, but the stated reason is to make people decide not to try.
The guard is not standing in for another control that the firm cannot use.
Making people decide not to try is discouraging the attempt, which is deterrence.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

stem: A trading firm's handbook states that sharing a trading password will lead to demotion. Nothing in the trading systems stops a trader from sharing one.
ask: Which of the following control types does the threat of demotion serve?
why: Nothing stops a trader from sharing, so nothing is prevented.
The threat of demotion discourages sharing without stopping it.
The threat does not identify or record any sharing.
Nothing is repaired; the threat acts before any sharing.

stem: A technician arriving at a data center sees a sign on the door that reads: 'Unauthorized entry will be reported to the police.'
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the sign?
why: A sign telling people what to do would be directive, but this one warns of what happens.
The sign does not stop anyone opening the door.
The sign records nothing and raises no alert.
The sign warns of a consequence, which discourages entry.

stem: The HR director at a payroll company announces in the staff newsletter that an employee was dismissed for copying customer files to a personal drive. The aim is that others with the same idea decide not to try. Nothing about file access changes.
ask: Which of the following control types does the announcement serve?
why: The announcement finds no copying; it reports a case already handled.
Nothing about file access changes, so no copy is blocked.
It gives no instruction on how to handle files; it shows what happened to someone who broke the rule.
Showing the consequence works only on the decision to try, which is deterrence.

stem: The IT manager at a health clinic protects its remote admin portal only with a warning banner. An attacker who ignores the warning signs in with a stolen password.
ask: Which of the following control types would have stopped the sign-in?
why: The banner is already deterrent, and the attacker ignored it.
A preventive control blocks the action, which a warning cannot do.
Detection could notice the sign-in afterward but would not stop it.
Instructions rely on compliance, which this attacker ignores.

stem: When a records clerk at a county office opens a remote session to the records server, the session begins with the screen below.
ask: Which of the following control types does this screen provide?

lines: NOTICE: All sessions on this server are logged.
Misuse will be referred for prosecution.
Press Enter to continue.

why: The screen warns of prosecution to discourage misuse.
Pressing Enter lets anyone continue, so nothing is blocked.
The logging behind the screen is detective, but the screen itself only warns.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

stem: The owner of a self-storage business wants controls that discourage break-ins without blocking or recording anything.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: Signs warning that the site is monitored
Bright lights over the storage rows
An alarm log reviewed each morning
Replacing broken locks after a theft
why: Warning signs discourage an attempt without stopping it.
Bright lighting makes thieves feel seen, which discourages them.
Padlocks block entry, which is preventive.
Reviewing an alarm log identifies events, which is detective.
Repairing after a theft is corrective.

ask: Which of the following describes a preventive control?
options: It discourages an attempt without stopping it
It blocks an incident before it happens
It records an event so it can be investigated
It restores systems after an event
why: That describes a deterrent control.
Preventive controls stop the event before it occurs by restricting access or actions.
That describes a detective control.
That describes a corrective control.

ask: Which of the following controls is preventive?
options: A banner warning that misuse is prosecuted
why: Locking the account blocks further guessing.
A warning banner discourages but does not block, which is deterrent.
Log review identifies events after they happen, which is detective.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

stem: The operations manager at a bakery chain fits the stockroom with a door that stays locked until an employee enters the right code, so no one else can walk in.
ask: Which of the following control types does the coded lock provide?
why: The lock does not rely on anyone choosing to stay out; it keeps them out.
The lock does not record or alert; it blocks.
The lock blocks entry for anyone without the code.
Nothing has happened yet that needs repair.

stem: The IT contractor at a dental practice has set the firewall to drop every inbound connection from the internet to its patient database server before the connection reaches the server.
ask: Which of the following control types does the firewall provide here?
why: Dropping the connection stops it rather than only reporting it.
Dropping the connection before it arrives blocks it.
Nothing depends on the sender choosing to stop; the connection is refused.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

stem: A university's network engineer places a sensor in line with campus traffic. The sensor drops any packet that matches a known attack pattern.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the sensor?
why: The sensor drops the matching packets, which blocks the attack.
The sensor does identify attack patterns, but it also drops the packets, which goes past detection.
Nothing here relies on discouraging the attacker.
The sensor acts before the packet arrives, not after damage.

stem: The IT administrator at a veterinary clinic sets the booking system to lock any account after five wrong passwords in a row. No one has tried to guess a password yet.
ask: Which of the following control types does this setting provide?
why: Nothing has gone wrong yet; corrective controls act after an event to restore normal operation.
The lockout stops further guesses rather than only recording them.
The lockout is a standard safeguard in its own right, not a substitute for one that cannot be used.
Locking the account stops a password-guessing attempt before it can succeed.

stem: The office manager at a law office turns on full-disk encryption on its laptops so that the files on a stolen laptop cannot be read.
ask: Which of the following control types does the encryption provide?
why: Encryption does not record or report a theft.
Encryption is in place before any theft; corrective acts after.
Encryption prevents unauthorized reading of the files.
Encryption does not depend on discouraging a thief; it keeps the files unreadable.

stem: The desktop administrator at a payroll firm configures the workstations so that only programs on an approved list can start. Any other program is refused.
ask: Which of the following control types does this configuration provide?
why: A list of approved programs in a handbook would be directive; here the workstation refuses the rest.
The configuration blocks programs rather than only reporting them.
Programs not on the list are refused, so they never run.
Nothing here substitutes for a control that cannot be used.

stem: An administrator at a seafood exporter applies the rules below to the mail server's network interface.
ask: Which of the following control types does the second rule provide?

lines: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 192.0.2.25 eq 25
access-list 110 deny ip any host 192.0.2.25

why: The rule does not alert; it refuses the traffic.
No one is shown a warning; the traffic is simply blocked.
Nothing has gone wrong that needs repair.
The rule refuses all other traffic to the server before it arrives.

stem: A warehouse manager wants controls that actually stop an intruder getting in, rather than ones that only discourage or record an attempt.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: A No Entry sign on the fence
A locked gate at the loading bay
An access control vestibule at the entrance
why: A sign only instructs or discourages; it stops no one.
A camera records the attempt; it does not stop it.
Lighting discourages but does not block entry.
A locked gate blocks entry.
A vestibule holds a person until they are cleared, which blocks entry.

ask: Which of the following describes a compensating control?
options: A stand-in for a measure that cannot be used
A repair made after an incident has happened
A barrier that stops an event before it starts
An instruction telling people what to do
why: A compensating control gives similar protection when the required control cannot be put in place.
That describes a corrective control.
That describes a preventive control.
That describes a directive control.

ask: Which of the following situations calls for a compensating control?
options: An attack has already caused damage
An attacker should be discouraged from trying
An event must be spotted as it happens
A required safeguard cannot be put in place
why: Repairing damage after an attack calls for a corrective control.
Discouraging attempts calls for a deterrent control.
Spotting events calls for a detective control.
Compensating controls exist for exactly this case.

stem: A city's traffic signal controller runs firmware that cannot accept security updates. Until the controller is replaced, the city's traffic engineer places it behind a firewall that admits connections from just two engineering laptops.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the firewall arrangement?
why: The firewall does block traffic, but it is there because the updates cannot be applied.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The firewall stands in for the security updates the controller cannot accept.
The firewall enforces access; it does not just tell people what to do.

stem: A two-person accounting office cannot split payment duties between different people. To make up for this, the owner reviews every payment record at the end of each day.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the owner's daily review?
why: Reviewing records is detective work, but it is done because the duties cannot be split.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The review stands in for the separation of duties the office cannot have.
The review does not tell anyone what to do.

stem: A factory's milling machine runs software that cannot run antivirus. Until the machine is replaced, the plant manager keeps it off the network and loads files onto it only from one checked USB drive.
ask: Which of the following control types does the plant's arrangement provide?
why: No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The arrangement is enforced, not just an instruction to staff.
Nothing here aims to discourage an attacker.
Keeping the machine off the network stands in for the antivirus it cannot run.

stem: A water utility's standard requires multifactor sign-in, but its old billing application cannot support it. The utility's IT manager now has users reach the application only through a gateway server that does require multifactor sign-in.
ask: Which of the following describes the role the gateway plays here?
options: It repairs the software after a breach
It stands in for a feature the app lacks
It records each sign-in for later review
It tells staff how to sign in safely
why: Nothing was breached; repairing after an event would be corrective.
The gateway gives the multifactor protection the application itself cannot provide, which is compensating.
The gateway enforces a second factor; it does not only record sign-ins.
Users are not just told what to do; the gateway enforces the second factor.

stem: A facilities manager at a translation agency must add badge readers to every server room door under the company's security standard. The lease of the office building forbids any wiring through the doors, so under an approved exception the manager instead keeps the servers in locked cabinets whose keys sit in a logged key safe.
ask: Which of the following control types do the locked cabinets provide in this case?
why: No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The cabinets stand in for the badge readers the lease does not allow, guarding the same servers.
The cabinets physically keep people out; they are not instructions to staff.
The cabinets are not there to discourage anyone; they replace the required readers.

stem: A jeweler's insurer requires that any after-hours entry to the stock room be detected and answered within minutes, and recommends a night guard, which the shop cannot afford. With the insurer's written approval, the store manager instead installs a door alarm monitored by a firm that sends a responder within minutes.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the alarm in this case?
why: The alarm meets the same requirement the guard would have met, in place of a guard the shop cannot afford.
The alarm detects entry, but it was put in place instead of the guard the insurer recommended and meets the same requirement.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The alarm does not tell anyone what to do.

stem: An auditor at a museum reads the exception record below.
ask: Which of the following describes the in_place_instead line?

lines: required: full-disk encryption on all devices
asset: GALLERY-KIOSK-2 (hardware cannot support encryption)
in_place_instead: no visitor data stored locally, kiosk bolted to the wall
review: quarterly

options: A repair made after an earlier incident
A substitute for a missing safeguard
why: No incident is recorded; nothing is being repaired.
The line lists measures in place, not instructions to staff.
The line lists what stands in for the encryption the kiosk cannot support, which is compensating.
Nothing in the line identifies or records events.

stem: A risk analyst at a logistics firm reviews a colleague's summary of compensating controls.
ask: Which of the following statements in the summary are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: It is applied after an incident to restore systems
It addresses the same risk as the missing control
It is any cheaper control chosen to save money
It is often temporary until the ideal control is possible
It only tells staff what they should do
why: Restoring after an incident is corrective.
A compensating control must give similar protection against the same risk.
It must address the same risk to a comparable degree; cost alone does not make one.
It is often a stand-in until the system can take the ideal control.
Telling staff what to do is directive.
